items.prompt: Describe how sharing a story digitally is different from sharing it on paper. Give TWO differences.
items.answer: Difference 1: Digital sharing allows many people to read the story at the same time on their own devices, while a paper copy can only be read by one person at a time unless many copies are printed. Difference 2: Digital sharing can happen instantly from anywhere by sending a file or link, while paper sharing requires the document to be physically delivered.

steps: Think about reach: how many people, how far.
Think about speed: how fast can each type be shared.

items.prompt: A student is deciding whether to write her science report by hand or type it. She needs to submit it to her teacher and two classmates for feedback. Which method is better and why?
items.answer: Typing is better because she can easily send the file to her teacher and classmates by email or shared document. They can all read and comment on it without her making three copies. Digital sharing is faster and more efficient for getting feedback from multiple people.

steps: Handwriting: she would need to make three copies or pass one around.
Typing: she sends the file once and all three can access it simultaneously.

items.prompt: What does 'collaboration' mean? Describe how TWO students could use a digital tool to write a story together.
items.answer: Collaboration means two or more people working together on a shared goal. For example, two students could open a shared document on the school's tablet. Student 1 types the beginning of the story while Student 2 watches. Then Student 2 types the middle while Student 1 reads and suggests edits. They take turns until the story is complete, then they both review it before submitting.

steps: Define collaboration clearly.
Describe a step-by-step process that shows both students contributing using a digital tool.

items.prompt: Explain the digital publishing process from start to finish. What steps does a student take to publish a story digitally?
items.answer: Step 1: Draft — the student writes the story (may start on paper or type directly). Step 2: Revise — the student rereads and improves the content. Step 3: Edit — check for spelling, capitalization, and punctuation. Step 4: Type the final version on a computer if not already typed. Step 5: Save the file. Step 6: Publish — post to the class website, email to the teacher, or upload to a shared folder for others to read.

steps: The writing process ends in publishing.
Digital publishing adds specific steps: saving, uploading, or emailing.

items.prompt: Think about a class that makes a digital book of all their writing. Why is this a good learning activity? Give two reasons.
items.answer: Reason 1: Students can read each other's writing and learn from different ideas and styles. Reason 2: Publishing gives students a real audience, which motivates them to do their best work. Seeing their writing shared also teaches them that writing has a purpose beyond just completing an assignment.

steps: Think about what students gain from reading peer writing and from having their own work published.
Consider motivation, community, and skill development.

items.prompt: A student's family does not have a computer at home. How could she still participate in a digital writing project at school?
items.answer: She could use a computer at school during class time or free time in the school computer lab. The library may also have public computers. Her teacher could also print a copy for her so she can read her peers' work even without a home computer.

steps: School computers, library computers, and printed alternatives ensure all students can participate.
The digital divide is real; teachers should offer alternatives.

items.prompt: What are THREE keys on a keyboard that you would use most often when writing a sentence, and what does each do?
items.answer: 1. Letter keys: press each letter to type the words in the sentence. 2. Space bar: press it to add a space between each word. 3. Shift key: hold it while pressing a letter to make it a capital at the start of a sentence or for proper nouns. Bonus: Enter key to start a new paragraph.

steps: Letter keys = typing.
Space bar = separating words.
Shift = capitalization.

items.prompt: Imagine a student publishes her story on the class website. Three things can now happen that could not happen if she handed in a paper copy to her teacher. What are they?
items.answer: 1. Many people (classmates, parents, family members) can read it at the same time from anywhere in the world. 2. The story can be read again and again without wearing out. 3. People who are far away, like grandparents in another city, can read it without needing a printed copy mailed to them.

steps: Wide reach: many readers simultaneously.
Durability: digital files do not wear out.
Distance: accessible globally.

items.prompt: A student typed a paragraph but noticed she made a spelling error in the third word. She does not want to delete everything she typed after the error. What is the most efficient way to fix it on the keyboard?
items.answer: The most efficient way is to click with the mouse or tap on the screen right before the misspelled word. This moves the cursor to that spot. Then she can use the backspace key to delete only the wrong word and retype it correctly, without touching anything else she already typed.

steps: Click to move the cursor to the error location.
Use backspace to delete only the misspelled word.
Retype the correct word.
Continue from there without deleting anything else.

items.prompt: Write a paragraph explaining to a student who has never used a computer why typing their story on a computer is useful.
items.answer: Typing your story on a computer is useful for many reasons. First, when you make a mistake, you can press the backspace key and retype the correct letter without any erasing or crossing out. Second, when your story is finished, you can share it with your teacher, your classmates, and even your family just by sending a file, without printing anything. Third, your story is saved on the computer so you will never lose it even if you forget to put it in your backpack. Learning to type is a skill that will help you in school and in life.

steps: Explain fixing mistakes.
Explain sharing.
Explain saving.
Motivate with real-world usefulness.

items.prompt: What is the difference between 'typing' and 'publishing'? Are they the same thing?
items.answer: Typing is the act of pressing keys to create a document on the screen. Publishing is the step where the finished, revised, and edited document is shared with an audience. They are not the same: you can type without publishing (if you save it privately), and in the past people published by printing without typing (using a printing press). Publishing always involves an audience; typing does not.

steps: Typing = mechanical process of entering text.
Publishing = sharing finished work with readers.
Typing comes before publishing in the process.

items.prompt: Explain how a tablet with a touch keyboard works differently from a desktop keyboard. Which might be harder for a first grader and why?
items.answer: A desktop keyboard has physical keys that you press down with your fingers, which gives you a click feeling to confirm each letter was typed. A tablet touch keyboard shows keys on the screen and you tap them with your fingertip, but there is no click feeling. A desktop keyboard might be easier for a first grader because the physical feedback (the click) makes it clearer that a letter was pressed, and the larger keys are easier to hit accurately.

steps: Physical keyboard: tactile feedback, larger keys.
Touch keyboard: flat screen, relies on sight more than feel.
Physical feedback helps beginning typers.

items.prompt: A student says: 'Typing is harder than writing by hand, so I do not want to use a computer.' Write a response that explains why learning to type is still worth the effort.
items.answer: Learning to type can be hard at first because you have to find each letter key. However, the more you practice, the faster and easier it becomes. When you can type quickly, you can write more in less time, fix mistakes instantly, and share your work with anyone in the world. Most jobs, schools, and daily activities today require computer skills, so the effort you put in now will pay off for the rest of your life.

steps: Acknowledge the challenge.
Explain that it gets easier with practice.
Give real reasons why typing skills matter in the long run.

items.prompt: What is one way digital writing tools can help students with disabilities? Give a specific example.
items.answer: Digital writing tools can help students who have difficulty with handwriting due to motor challenges. For example, a student who finds it hard to form letters neatly with a pencil can type clearly legible text on a keyboard. Some tablets also have voice-to-text features that allow a student to speak and have their words automatically typed on the screen.

steps: Think about who might benefit most from not needing to handwrite.
Voice-to-text and keyboard typing both bypass handwriting challenges.

items.prompt: Imagine your class creates a digital poem collection. Describe the whole process from writing to publishing, including all the steps.
items.answer: Step 1: Each student writes a poem on paper first (drafting). Step 2: Students revise their poems with their teacher's help. Step 3: Students edit for spelling and punctuation. Step 4: Students type their final poems on a computer or tablet. Step 5: The teacher collects all the typed poems into one digital document. Step 6: The teacher formats the document to look like a real poetry book. Step 7: The document is published on the class website or emailed to all families. Step 8: Families and friends read the digital poetry collection on their devices.

steps: Follow the writing process: draft, revise, edit.
Then move to digital steps: type, collect, format, publish, share.
